name: Stereotype threat
statement: Being at risk of confirming a negative stereotype about one's own group depresses performance on a test in the stereotyped domain.
meaning: The claim is about a situation, not a person. A Black student sitting a verbal test described as diagnostic of intellectual ability, or a woman sitting a maths test described as producing gender differences, faces the prospect of being judged by a stereotype. Steele and Aronson argued that this prospect consumes attention and lowers the score. Two predictions follow. Members of the stereotyped group should score lower when the stereotype is made relevant than when it is not, and changing the description of the test should change the score without changing anything about the taker.

origin.who: Claude M. Steele and Joshua Aronson
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Four experiments on Black and White Stanford undergraduates taking difficult verbal items. The paper coined the term and set the template every later study follows: one group told the test measures ability, another told it does not.

evidence: Steele and Aronson ran four small experiments. Study 1 recruited 117 undergraduates across three conditions and analysed 114 after three failed to give a SAT score. The analysis was an ANCOVA with self-reported SAT scores as the covariate, and the race-by-condition interaction did not reach conventional significance, p < .19. A weighted contrast dropping the challenge conditions gave F(1, 107) = 3.27, p < .08, which the authors called marginal. Study 2 used 40 female undergraduates, 10 per cell, and there the race-by-diagnosticity interaction on adjusted test performance was significant, F(1, 35) = 8.07, p < .01. Study 3 used 68 students. Study 4 assigned 47 and analysed 44 after three exclusions, and it showed that merely asking students to record their race before the test lowered Black students' scores, F(1, 39) = 7.82, p < .01. Spencer, Steele and Quinn extended the design to women and mathematics in 1999. Their Study 2 gave 30 women and 24 men at Michigan two halves of a hard test, describing one half as producing gender differences, and Study 3 repeated the pattern at Buffalo with 36 women and 31 men on an easier test. That paper is what the schoolgirl literature grew out of. Roughly one hundred research papers and five meta-analyses followed for the gender version alone, by Flore and Wicherts' count. Those five estimated a small to medium effect before moderators, with standardised mean differences from 0.24 to 0.48, as Flore and Wicherts summarise them.

examples.tag: The maths paper introduced as a gender comparison
examples.text: A teacher hands out a hard paper and mentions that the exercise is being used to look at how boys and girls differ. On this account the girls now sit the paper with the prospect of confirming a stereotype in mind, and that prospect takes attention the questions needed.

examples.tag: The boxes ticked before the first question
examples.text: An assessment opens by asking candidates to record their ethnicity, then describes itself as a measure of raw ability. Nothing about the questions has changed. What is claimed is that the framing alone moves the score of a candidate whose group the test is stereotyped against.

examples.tag: The memory screen at the clinic
examples.text: An older patient is told that a short recall task is the standard check for age-related decline. The proposal holds that being measured against the stereotype of the forgetful old takes up part of what the patient needs in order to do the recalling.

replication.headline: A preregistered test on 2,064 Dutch high-school students found no stereotype threat effect on girls' maths scores, with the Bayes factor favouring the null by 28 to 1.
replication.detail: Flore and Wicherts pooled 47 effect sizes from studies of schoolgirls taking maths, science and spatial tests, covering 3,760 girls. The random-effects estimate was g = -0.22, 95% CI -0.34 to -0.10. Their publication-bias tests then undercut it. Trim and fill imputed 11 missing effect sizes and dropped the estimate to g = -0.07, 95% CI -0.21 to 0.06, no longer distinguishable from zero. Egger's test gave z = -3.25, p = .001, and studies with fewer than 60 participants gave g = -0.34 against g = -0.13 for the larger ones. They called for a large replication and then ran it. The registered report reached 86 classes at 21 Dutch schools and analysed 2,064 students from the 2,126 tested. Adding the stereotype threat manipulation to the model, and then its interaction with gender, did not improve model fit. The interaction coefficient was 0.16 with a standard error of 0.31. The default Bayes factor for the no-threat hypothesis against the stereotype threat hypothesis was 28.18, and the posterior probability of the null was .963. Two later results point the same way. Inglis and O'Hagan gave 1,169 English schoolchildren answer sheets asking their gender before or after a maths challenge, and the predicted interaction gave F(1, 1165) = 0.525, p = .469, with girls scoring slightly higher in the gender-first condition. A registered replication report by Stoevenbelt and 21 colleagues ran nine direct replications of Johns, Schmader and Martens across eight labs. It collected 1,795 participants and analysed 1,709, of whom 74.61% were women. Among those women the effect was g = 0.04, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.20, against d = -0.82 in the original 45-person study.

study.cite: Flore, P. C., Mulder, J., & Wicherts, J. M. (2018). The influence of gender stereotype threat on mathematics test scores of Dutch high school students: a registered report. Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology, 3(2), 140-174.

limits: The record above is about schoolgirls and maths. For adults on cognitive ability tests the picture is graded rather than flat, and Shewach, Sackett and Quint's meta-analysis of 212 samples is the place to read it. Excluding the studies that adjust for a prior ability score, the pooled effect was d = -0.31 across 181 samples and 10,436 people, with a 90% credibility interval from -0.93 to 0.32. Restricting the set to the 45 samples whose conditions resemble a real testing session, meaning subtle rather than blatant threat cues, total-correct scoring, a plain control group and no ability covariate, gave d = -0.14 across 3,532 people. Trim and fill cut that to -0.09 and the interval crossed zero. The four samples drawn from actual college placement exams gave d = -0.01 across 1,670 people, against d = -0.36 in the 177 laboratory samples. Studies offering money to top performers gave d = 0.00. Published studies in that database showed an effect more than twice the size of unpublished ones, -0.37 against -0.17. The one figure this entry has for ethnic minority test-takers on their own, d = -0.26 across 35 samples and 2,432 people, is a moderator row of that same database rather than a separate meta-analysis. Searches of Crossref, OpenAlex, OSF preprints and the open web on 21 September 2026 located no comparable preregistered multi-site replication of the race version of the effect.
misreadings: The most consequential error is not about whether the effect exists. Steele and Aronson analysed test scores with prior SAT scores held constant, so their finding of no Black-White difference in the non-diagnostic condition means that students matched on prior SAT performed alike, not that the raw gap disappeared. In Study 2 the mean SAT score was 655 for White participants and 603 for Black participants. Sackett, Hardison and Cullen counted how often this was reported as the gap being eliminated. Ten of the 11 journal articles and chapters that described the study got it wrong, or 90.9%, as did five of the nine introductory psychology textbooks that made Black-White comparisons, or 55.6%. Their article is paywalled and was not obtained here, and those two counts come from a University of Chicago teaching handout that reproduces them. Steele and Aronson did not make the error themselves. Tomeh and Sackett repeated the audit over 2005 to 2019 and found the rate had fallen to 62.8% of the 94 journal articles that discussed between-group comparisons, and to seven of 17 such textbooks, or 41.18%. Reading the replication record as proof that stereotype threat is nothing is the opposite error. Shewach and colleagues put it as a shift in the burden of proof rather than a refutation, and their own focal estimate before bias correction was small and negative, not zero.

sources.text: Steele, C. M., & Aronson, J. (1995). Stereotype threat and the intellectual test performance of African Americans. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 69(5), 797-811. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from the open copy Stanford SPARQ serves. Every figure above was taken off it: the 117 recruited and 114 analysed, the p < .19 interaction, F(1, 107) = 3.27 for the weighted contrast, the 40 participants and F(1, 35) = 8.07 in Study 2, the 68 in Study 3, the 47 assigned and 11 per cell in Study 4 with F(1, 39) = 7.82, and the 655 and 603 SAT means.

Spencer, S. J., Steele, C. M., & Quinn, D. M. (1999). Stereotype Threat and Women's Math Performance. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 35(1), 4-28. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from an open copy at hendrix.edu, whose title page carries the article's own page range of 4 to 28. A previous version of this entry called it paywalled and unread, and described it from Flore and Wicherts' summary instead. The participant counts for Studies 2 and 3 are read off it.

Flore, P. C., & Wicherts, J. M. (2015). Does stereotype threat influence performance of girls in stereotyped domains? A meta-analysis. Journal of School Psychology, 53(1), 25-44. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from the author's own copy at jeltewichertsdotnet.files.wordpress.com. The 47 effect sizes, the 3,760 girls, g = -0.22, the 11 imputed effect sizes, g = -0.07, Egger's z = -3.25, the -0.34 against -0.13 split at 60 participants, the hundred papers, the five meta-analyses and the 0.24 to 0.48 range are all in it. Note that the paper gives 0.48 on page 26 and 0.45 later for the same Walton and Spencer estimate.

Flore, P. C., Mulder, J., & Wicherts, J. M. (2018). The influence of gender stereotype threat on mathematics test scores of Dutch high school students: a registered report. Comprehensive Results in Social Psychology, 3(2), 140-174. Read in full on 21 September 2026. Taylor and Francis and the Tilburg research portal both answer with a Cloudflare challenge, not a paywall, and the Wayback Machine was unreachable all day. The file came from the legacy Tilburg host pure.uvt.nl on its portalfiles path. The 21 schools, 86 classes, 2,126 tested and 2,064 analysed, the 0.16 coefficient with its 0.31 standard error, the Bayes factor of 28.177 and the posterior probability of .963 were all read off it.

Shewach, O. R., Sackett, P. R., & Quint, S. (2019). Stereotype threat effects in settings with features likely versus unlikely in operational test settings: A meta-analysis. Journal of Applied Psychology, 104(12), 1514-1534. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from the copy gwern.net mirrors, which is the advance online version rather than the paginated 104(12) one. Table 2 carries every figure quoted here, including the focal sample's definition in footnote a and the note in footnote c that all four operational samples were college placement examinations. The burden-of-proof sentence is in its discussion.

Inglis, M., & O'Hagan, S. (2022). Stereotype threat, gender and mathematics attainment: A conceptual replication of Stricker & Ward. PLOS ONE, 17(5), e0267699. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from the PLOS printable PDF. The 1,169 figure is the analysed sample, after 44 students who ignored the invigilation instructions and 23 who gave no gender were dropped. F(1, 1165) = 0.525, p = .469 and the higher gender-first means for girls are in its results.

Stoevenbelt, A. H., Flore, P. C., Wicherts, J. M., et al. (2025). Registered Replication Report: Johns, Schmader, & Martens (2005). PsyArXiv preprint, version 5, posted 18 December 2025, in press at Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science. Read in full on 21 September 2026. The OSF download path returns an application shell, and the file came from api.osf.io. Its own title page says the manuscript is in press at Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, so it is not unreviewed. A previous version of this entry gave version 1's figures under version 5's identifier: version 1, posted 17 September 2024, reports eight replications, N = 1502 and 822 women with d = -0.006, while version 5 reports nine replications across eight labs, 1,709 analysed and g = 0.04 among women. Crossref held no journal version on 21 September 2026.

Sackett, P. R., Hardison, C. M., & Cullen, M. J. (2004). On Interpreting Stereotype Threat as Accounting for African American-White Differences on Cognitive Tests. American Psychologist, 59(1), 7-13. Not obtained. The American Psychological Association's copy is paywalled, and Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, the University of Minnesota research portal and open-web search turned up no free copy on 21 September 2026. ResearchGate answered with a captcha. The 90.9% and the five of nine textbooks quoted here were read off a University of Chicago Econ 341 teaching handout that reproduces the paper's three audits verbatim.

Tomeh, D. H., & Sackett, P. R. (2022). On the Continued Misinterpretation of Stereotype Threat as Accounting for Black-White Differences on Cognitive Tests. Personnel Assessment and Decisions, 8(1), article 1. Read in full on 21 September 2026 from the copy gwern.net mirrors, after ScholarWorks at Bowling Green answered every request for its PDF with a Cloudflare challenge. Its own denominators are 94 journal articles and 17 textbooks addressing between-group comparisons. Its one-line summary of Sackett and colleagues drops the textbook denominator, and an earlier version of this entry inherited that looseness.
